# 18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability

Part of [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/Backend from First Principles|Backend from First Principles]] · Previous: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/17 Configuration Management/17 Configuration Management|17 Configuration Management]] · Next: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/19 Graceful Shutdown/19 Graceful Shutdown|19 Graceful Shutdown]]

Once a backend is running in production, you need a way to know **what it is doing**, **whether it is healthy**, and **why it broke** when something goes wrong. Logging, monitoring and observability are the practices that answer these questions. Each one is big enough to be its own course; this lesson gives a practical overview and then walks through a real Go application that uses them.

Unlike most lessons in this series, this one looks at code. These are practices that live inside the code, so they are hard to understand without seeing them.

## 1. Why we need these practices

Modern backends run in a **distributed environment**:

- the application runs on **many servers**, often in **several regions**,
- it talks to databases, caches, queues and external services,
- its users are spread across the world.

When something goes wrong in a setup like that, you cannot just "look at the server". You need practices, tools and methods to **keep track of what is happening** across all services and infrastructure.

### It is a spectrum, not a checklist

There are no fixed rules here. Companies and teams adopt these practices **to different degrees**. No product can honestly claim to follow *every* good logging, monitoring and observability practice. Keep this in mind so the huge number of tools, products and buzzwords in this area doesn't feel intimidating.

> [!note] Scope
> These practices apply to frontend applications too, but this note sticks to the backend.

---

## 2. Short definitions

### Logging

**Logging** means **recording important events** that happen in the application, such as:

- normal important events (a user logs in, a to-do is created),
- suspicious events,
- security-related events,
- errors (a database query fails).

Each log entry carries **metadata**, extra context that helps later. For example:

- which **user ID** triggered the request,
- the **latency** (how long the request took),
- which **function or method** handled it,
- a **timestamp**.

Think of logs as a **diary** the backend keeps, so that later you can find out **what happened, when, and why**. Logging covers the whole life cycle: application startup, every request, and shutdown.

### Monitoring

**Monitoring** means **continuously checking the health and performance** of the system, for example:

- the server's **CPU** and **memory** usage,
- **requests per second** being processed,
- the state of **database connections**, such as how many pooled connections are open (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/12 Databases with Postgres/12 Databases with Postgres|lesson 12]]).

Monitoring gives you **near-real-time** data, plus patterns over time (how the system behaved over the last hour, day or week).

"Real time" here usually means a **delay of around 10–15 seconds**. Some tools can get down to seconds or milliseconds, but traditional setups collect data in intervals so they don't overwhelm the monitoring system with a constant stream of data.

### Observability

A system is **observable** if you can **work out its internal state by looking at its external outputs**.

In practice, observability rests on **three pillars**. A backend is only called observable when all three are in place:

| Pillar | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Logs** | Records of the important events across startup, requests and shutdown. |
| **Metrics** | Numbers that describe the system over time (closely tied to monitoring). |
| **Traces** | The path of a single request through the system's components. |

#### Traces

A **trace** is like a **transaction** for one request. It records:

- **where the request started**: the frontend, a load balancer, or the backend itself,
- **every component it passed through**, for example:

```text
handler → validation → service → repository → database
```

(These layers are covered in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context|lesson 10]].)

So a trace shows the full journey of one request, including every component involved.

---

## 3. Monitoring vs observability

Observability as a practice is **fairly new**, a matter of a few years. About a decade ago, catching problems at the infrastructure level relied mostly on **traditional monitoring**.

| | Traditional monitoring | Observability |
|---|---|---|
| Tells you **that** something is wrong | ✅ (via alerts, e.g. set up in Grafana) | ✅ |
| Tells you **what exactly** is wrong and where | ❌ You only get informed | ✅ If logs, metrics and traces are all implemented |

The weakness of monitoring alone: you get an alert saying "something is wrong with your application", and then you are on your own. Observability adds the context (logs and traces) to go from the alert straight to the cause.

See also [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/16 Error Handling and Fault-Tolerant Systems/16 Error Handling and Fault-Tolerant Systems#3. Monitoring and observability|monitoring and observability in lesson 16]].

---

## 4. How logs, metrics and traces work together

Each pillar answers a different question:

| Source | Tells you |
|---|---|
| **Logs** | **What** exactly happened |
| **Metrics** (from monitoring) | **Patterns and trends** |
| **Traces** (from observability) | **How components interacted** |

### What metrics are

**Metrics** are **concrete numbers** about the system, current or historical. Examples:

- how many requests were processed,
- how many requests **failed**, meaning they returned an error status code (4xx or 5xx),
- business numbers: in a to-do app, how many to-dos were created and how many creations failed,
- these numbers over a window: the last 30 minutes, the last hour, and so on.

You **decide in advance** which metrics you care about, both in your code and in whichever tool you use.

### A typical debugging workflow

This is how it usually goes in a production system that has all three pillars set up:

1. **Alert.** You configured a rule such as "if the error rate goes above X%, notify us". When it fires, a message arrives in **Slack** (usually through a **webhook**): "Something is wrong with the API service."
2. **Metrics.** You open the dashboard and confirm it: the error rate really is high.
3. **Logs.** From the metric, the tool shows you the **logs related to it**, e.g. all the failed requests.
4. **Traces.** You click a log, say one with a 500 error, and see its **trace**: the request started in this function, moved to that function, then to another, and **failed at this exact point**.
5. **Fix.** You now know exactly where things went wrong and can debug it right away.

Going from alert to the exact failing line in a few clicks is the whole benefit of implementing these practices.

> [!example] Illustrative threshold
> The example threshold was "error rate above 80%". Real alerts are often set much lower (a few percent), depending on the service. Pick thresholds that fit your system.

---

## 5. Tools: open source vs all-in-one

| Approach | Tools | When it fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Open source** (the "Grafana stack") | **Prometheus** builds and stores metrics; **Grafana** is the dashboard (frontend) and alerting; **Loki** with **Promtail** handles logs; **Jaeger** handles traces | Common in enterprises; flexible, but you must run and maintain many tools |
| **ELK stack** | **Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana** for collecting, parsing and searching logs | Log management |
| **Proprietary all-in-one** | **New Relic**, **Datadog**, etc. | Simpler integration; good when you lack the team size, time or experience to maintain the open-source tools |

Setting all of this up yourself is complicated. If you don't have the experience or time, a proprietary all-in-one service is often the more sensible choice. The demo app in this lesson uses **New Relic** for exactly that reason.

---

## 6. Log levels

Most logging libraries let you give each log entry a **level**, which says how important it is. The common levels, from least to most severe:

| Level | Used for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **debug** | Detailed information while troubleshooting in **development**. Can be overwhelming, so usually **disabled in production**. | "To-do created with ID 42" with all internal details |
| **info** | Normal operations, **successful** actions and **business events**. | `log.info("todo created")` |
| **warn** | Between info and error: not a success, but **not serious enough to be an error**, and often not your system's fault. | A user typed the wrong password and authentication failed |
| **error** | Real failures. The most common reason to log at all. | A validation error, a failed database query |
| **fatal** | A very serious problem; the application **stops** after logging it, and may be restarted by the infrastructure. | The app can't start or continue at all |

Filtering by level is how you keep production logs useful: in production you typically log **info and above**, in development you log **debug and above**. The log level is usually a configuration value (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/17 Configuration Management/17 Configuration Management#3. Types of configuration|lesson 17]]).

---

## 7. Structured vs unstructured logs

There are two main ways to print logs.

### Unstructured (console) logs: for development

When you run the backend locally, logs go to your terminal or editor console. Here you want them:

- **human-readable** plain text,
- **attractive**, e.g. with colours,

because that makes it easy to spot and fix issues.

```text
10:15:02 INF connected to database
10:15:02 INF started background job server
10:15:02 INF starting server port=8080
```

### Structured (JSON) logs: for production

**Structured logging** means each log entry is printed in a machine-readable format, almost always **JSON**, with named fields:

```json
{"level":"error","time":"2026-11-03T10:15:02Z","request_id":"a1b2c3","user_id":"u_42","method":"GET","path":"/todos","status":401,"message":"unauthorized"}
```

This is hard for a person to read in a terminal, but in production your logs are fed into a **log management tool** (ELK, the Grafana stack, New Relic…). Those tools need to **parse** the logs and pull out fields such as user ID or request ID.

- Parsing free text is error-prone and inefficient.
- Parsing JSON is easy and reliable.

| Environment | Format | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Development | Unstructured console text | Easy for humans to read and spot errors |
| Production | Structured JSON | Easy for tools to parse and give insights |

> [!example] Illustrative output
> The two log samples above are illustrative. They show the shape of each format, not the demo app's exact output.

---

## 8. Demo: setting up the logger

The demo is a **to-do application** with a backend written in **Go**, wired up to **New Relic**. The point is to see the practices in action, not to memorise the code.

One file creates the **logger** before the application starts. Two of its settings match the theory above.

### Log level depends on the environment

A function `getLogLevel` checks the environment:

- **local / development** → **debug** level, for more detail while debugging,
- **production** → **info** level, only information-related logs and above.

### Log format: console or JSON

The format is a setting:

- **console** by default, since the default environment is development,
- **json** for production.

Observed in the demo:

- With the format switched to **JSON** and the environment to production, the server printed all its startup logs as **JSON**: fine for tools, hard to read.
- Switched back to the development setup (**console**), the same startup logs were clearly readable: first **connecting to the database**, then **starting the background job server**, then **starting the server**.

---

## 9. Instrumentation and OpenTelemetry

Two terms come up constantly when talking about observability.

### Instrumentation

**Instrumentation** is the practice of adding code that **measures and records** what your functions do: how long they take, what attributes they had, whether they failed. It is what makes a system observable.

In the demo, the router uses a **New Relic middleware** that wraps the whole app. On every incoming request it **instruments** that request automatically. (Middlewares are covered in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context#6. Middlewares|lesson 10]].)

### OpenTelemetry

**OpenTelemetry** (often shortened to **OTel**) is an **open standard** for instrumentation. It is a relatively recent addition and provides a whole ecosystem:

- APIs and **SDKs** for all major languages (Node.js, Go, Python, …),
- tools such as the **OpenTelemetry Collector**, which receives telemetry data and forwards it to a backend,
- best practices and resources.

Because it is a standard, it doesn't tie you to one vendor. Even with a proprietary tool like New Relic, you can add an OpenTelemetry collector to get more control over how requests and components are instrumented.

---

## 10. Demo: following one request through the code

### Step 1: a middleware starts the transaction

A middleware called **enhanced tracing** is the **first point of contact** in the request's life cycle. It:

1. creates a new **transaction** using New Relic's API,
2. attaches attributes to it:
   - the **service name** (from configuration),
   - the **environment** (local or production),
   - the client's **IP address** and **user agent**,
   - the **request ID**,
   - the **user ID**, **user email** and **tenant ID**,
3. stores the transaction in the **request context** (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context#9. Request context|lesson 10]]).

Because the transaction travels in the context, every later layer (validation, service, repository) can add to the **same trace**. One request → one trace, from the middleware all the way down.

### Step 2: the `CreateTodo` service

Inside the service that creates a to-do, the code does this, in order:

1. **Takes the transaction out of the context.**
2. **Starts a segment** for this function and arranges for it to **end when the function returns**. A segment is one timed step inside the trace, here "to-do create service".
3. **Adds attributes** to the transaction: the **user ID** and the **title** of the requested to-do.
4. **Logs the event**: the operation `create todo` with the title.
5. If the request payload included a **priority**, adds it as an attribute and logs it too.
6. Logs an **info** message that it is starting to create the to-do.
7. Runs some validation of the **parent/child** relationship between to-dos.
8. Runs the **database operation** that creates the to-do.
9. **On error**:
   - logs it at **error** level,
   - **attaches the error to the trace** through the transaction,
   - adds the attribute "operation = create" so the trace shows this operation failed.
10. **On success**:
    - adds attributes: operation = create, and the new to-do's **ID**,
    - logs at **debug** level that the to-do was created with that ID. This **won't appear in production**, because production logs info and above,
    - logs a **business event**, "todo created", with its metadata: ID, title, category ID and priority.

### What this looks like in code

The following is an **illustrative** Go-style sketch of the same pattern. It is not the demo's actual source.

```go
func (s *TodoService) CreateTodo(ctx context.Context, userID string, in CreateTodoInput) (*Todo, error) {
    txn := newrelic.FromContext(ctx)              // 1. transaction from context
    defer txn.StartSegment("todo.create").End()   // 2. segment ends when we return

    txn.AddAttribute("user_id", userID)           // 3. attributes for the trace
    txn.AddAttribute("todo_title", in.Title)
    log := s.logger.With().Str("operation", "create_todo").Str("title", in.Title).Logger()

    if in.Priority != nil {                       // 5. optional attribute
        txn.AddAttribute("priority", *in.Priority)
    }
    log.Info().Msg("creating todo")               // 6. info log

    todo, err := s.repo.Create(ctx, userID, in)   // 8. database operation
    if err != nil {                               // 9. error path
        log.Error().Err(err).Msg("failed to create todo")
        txn.NoticeError(err)
        return nil, err
    }

    txn.AddAttribute("todo_id", todo.ID)          // 10. success path
    log.Debug().Str("todo_id", todo.ID).Msg("todo created") // hidden in production
    log.Info().Str("event", "todo_created").Str("todo_id", todo.ID).Msg("business event")
    return todo, nil
}
```

The pattern to remember: **every important step leaves a log, and every useful fact is attached to the trace.**

---

## 11. Demo: the New Relic dashboard

For this part the app was switched to **JSON logs** and the **production** environment, so its logs would reach New Relic.

What was observed:

1. **Application overview.** It shows numbers such as **error rate** and **transaction time**. At first it was empty, because there had been no activity in the last 30 minutes.
2. **Generating traffic.** Using the app's **OpenAPI interface** (a web page for trying out the API), the "get all to-dos" endpoint was called several times **without a token**. Each call returned **401 Unauthorized**, which is exactly what we want to see logged.
3. **Errors → HTTP error type.** After a refresh, the **unauthorized errors** appeared, with their **related logs** listed alongside.
4. **Metrics (summary view).** Average **transaction time**, **throughput** and **errors**: actual numbers that quantify the system's state. The error rate was around **80%**, since most requests had been the unauthorized ones.
5. **A single log.** Clicking an unauthorized log showed all its context:
   - the application name and environment,
   - the error code (unauthorized),
   - the host name and IP,
   - the log level and message,
   - the HTTP method (GET) and route (`/todos`),
   - the **span ID** and timestamp.
6. **The trace.** The log is **linked to its trace**, which can be opened to see more detail. A **span** is one step within a trace; the span ID is what links a log line to the right place in the trace.
7. **Transactions.** The `/todos` transaction (the same transactions the code adds attributes to) shows its own error rate and response time.
8. **Go runtime.** Information about the environment the backend runs in: **garbage collection** time, **memory usage** (only about 3 MB here), throughput and average response time.

This is the whole loop from section 4 in practice: **metrics → logs → trace**.

---

## 12. A spectrum and a team effort

- No system is "100% observable" or logs and monitors every possible parameter. You implement these practices **to the degree that makes sense**.
- Whatever you pick, open source (Grafana, Loki, Prometheus, Jaeger) or proprietary (New Relic, Datadog), the dashboards only show what the **code actually records**. Without the instrumentation and logging calls from section 10, there would be nothing to see.
- It is a **collective effort**:
  - **developers** add logs, metrics and traces at the code level,
  - **infrastructure / DevOps** people set up the systems that collect logs, metrics and traces.
- There is no single special skill to learn here. The key is to remember that this is a very important part of any production backend.

---

## Key takeaways

- **Logging** records important events with context (user ID, request ID, latency, timestamp). It tells you **what happened**.
- **Monitoring** continuously tracks health and performance (CPU, memory, requests per second, connections). It tells you **that** something is wrong and shows **trends**.
- **Observability** means you can understand the internal state from the outputs. It rests on three pillars: **logs, metrics, traces**.
- A **trace** follows one request through every component; it shows **where** it failed.
- Workflow: **alert → metrics → logs → trace → fix**.
- Use **log levels**: debug (dev only), info, warn, error, fatal. Production typically logs info and above.
- Use **readable console logs in development** and **structured JSON logs in production**.
- **Instrumentation** is the code that measures your app. **OpenTelemetry** is the open, vendor-neutral standard for it.
- Tools: the open-source **Grafana stack** (Prometheus, Grafana, Loki/Promtail, Jaeger) or all-in-one services such as **New Relic** and **Datadog**.
- These practices exist on a **spectrum** and need both developers and DevOps.

---

## Review questions

1. Why is it harder to understand what's happening in a modern backend than in a single program on one machine?
2. What is logging? Give three kinds of metadata worth attaching to a log entry.
3. What does monitoring track? Give three examples.
4. Why is "real-time" monitoring data usually delayed by around 10–15 seconds?
5. When is a system called observable? Name the three pillars.
6. What is a trace, and which components might it pass through in a typical backend?
7. What can observability tell you that traditional monitoring alone cannot?
8. Match each pillar to the question it answers: what happened, what are the trends, how did components interact.
9. Describe the workflow from a Slack alert to finding the exact failing function.
10. What are metrics? Give one technical metric and one business metric for a to-do app.
11. Name the tools in the open-source Grafana stack and what each one does.
12. When might a team choose New Relic or Datadog over open-source tools?
13. Which log level would you use for: (a) a user typing the wrong password, (b) a failed database query, (c) a to-do being created, (d) detailed troubleshooting output?
14. Why is the debug level usually disabled in production?
15. Why do production systems log in JSON instead of plain text? Why not use JSON locally too?
16. What is instrumentation? What is OpenTelemetry, and why does it matter that it's an open standard?
17. In the demo, why is the transaction stored in the request context?
18. In the `CreateTodo` example, what happens to the trace when the database call fails?
19. In the dashboard demo, why was the error rate around 80%?
20. Why is logging, monitoring and observability a "collective effort"?

---

- [18. Logging, Monitoring and Observability](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5PEuwgLOQQM&list=PLui3EUkuMTPgZcV0QhQrOcwMPcBCcd_Q1). The provided transcript **ends mid-sentence** in the closing remarks ("a very important part of any production…"), so anything after that point is not covered.
- **Corrected names:** Grafana ("graphana"), Promtail ("Promptale"), Jaeger ("Jagger"), New Relic ("Newelic"), Datadog ("data dog"), OpenTelemetry ("open telemetry"), fatal ("fat"). ELK is expanded to Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana.
- **Clarifications:**
  - The transcript describes failed requests as "status code more than 200". The note uses the usual meaning, error status codes (4xx and 5xx). Some teams count only 5xx in their error rate.
  - The 80% alert threshold is the transcript's example; the note adds that real thresholds are usually much lower.
  - The definitions of *segment* and *span*, and the description of the OpenTelemetry Collector, are added for clarity.
- **Illustrative vs observed:**
  - **Illustrative:** the console and JSON log samples, the request path diagram, and the Go-style `CreateTodo` sketch (written for this note; the demo's real source is described only at the level the transcript gives).
  - **Observed in the demo:** the JSON vs console startup logs (database connection → background job server → server start), the 401 Unauthorized errors from calling get-all-to-dos without a token, the ~80% error rate, the log fields shown in New Relic, and memory usage of about 3 MB in the Go runtime view.
- **The creator's opinions:** choosing a proprietary all-in-one tool when you lack the team or experience for open-source tools, and the view that these practices exist on a spectrum.
